cim: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate
cim_eredeti: UM establishes Montana’s first artificial intelligence career certificate
szoveg_eredeti:
The University of Montana established a career certificate that intends to educate students about artificial intelligence this year, and students have mixed opinions.

The Human-Centered AI Career Certificate is the first of its kind in the state. Lee Banville, the director of the School of Journalism, and Michael Cassens, an associate professor of game design and interactive media, created the nine-credit certificate together and teach its three courses, all of which are taught online.

According to Banville, the purpose of the certificate is to teach students about AI and recognize that it will affect people’s lives and careers, not to promote or discourage its use.

“In no way is this a sales pitch for AI,” Banville said. “I’m not like, ‘You know what are great? Data centers.’ That’s not what this program or this certificate is about at all.”

Cassens said having the certificate would improve students’ resumes and give them knowledge that is needed in a technologically changing world.

“You will actually come out with a much deeper, stronger foundational knowledge base of not just how to work with AI, but how to actually talk about it effectively and with people that have varied feelings about it,” Cassens said.

He also said the use of AI for assignments would be required to earn the certificate. He intends to have his students use ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini, Meta and UM’s model, Chat MT, to explore how they work. One thing they could be expected to do, Cassens said, is put the same prompt into many models to see how the responses differ.

Cassens said that he expects that many of his students turn in assignments that incorporate AI somehow. As long as the student can reasonably defend their decision to use AI, he said he’s okay with it.

“I’m a huge fan of radical transparency,” Cassens said. “If you’re going to use artificial intelligence, say so and say why.”

The first course is Creatively Exploring AI, which is already offered and taught by Cassens. He said it’s focused on the history of AI, its hallucinations and biases, terminology, ethics and how specific disciplines could be affected by it.

The second is Calling Bullshit in the Age of AI, a journalism course that is currently offered under the name Calling Bullshit, but will change next semester. It’s taught by Banville, who said it focuses on critical thinking and knowing when AI is wrong.

The third is called Human-Centered Leadership in AI, a new class that will be offered in the spring by Cassens and is adapted from a leadership class he used to teach.

“We intentionally made this certificate really grounded in humanness because that’s what we do in this college,” Cassens said. “We are much more concerned about how human beings fit within all this.”

Cassens said the courses are made to be adaptable. As AI adapts and technology changes, so will the curriculum.

Grace Smith, a 23-year-old second-year graduate student studying game design, is already halfway through the certificate. She has taken Creatively Exploring AI and is currently in Calling Bullshit, and she said she thinks the courses are not pro or anti-artificial intelligence, but rather promote conversation about it.

“The students fill in gaps of opinion and are able to have that discourse amongst each other,” Smith said.

She said she wants to earn the certificate because AI is heavily pushed in corporate America.

“Having that critical thought process background to AI itself, instead of just offhand using it for automation, gives me an upper hand for myself and for my career path,” Smith said.

Kylie Heit, a 23-year-old senior cello performance major from Helena, said she doesn’t like AI. She thinks that the certificate, whether neutral or not, normalizes its use. She also said the “Human-Centered” title is a misnomer.

“There’s nothing human about AI,” Heit said. “AI should not be taking away our arts.”

Heit also said she doesn’t think any classes should require the use of AI, like the certificate courses do.

Andrew Bert, a junior anthropology major from Cedarburg, Wisconsin, said he sees potential in the new certificate program.

“Teaching people about how to use AI, how to use it correctly, and how to use it sustainably might be really good and it might help a lot of people,” Bert said.

Bert said he uses AI for research and to condense information for him, but he doesn’t use it to “completely do everything.”

Banville, the director of the School of Journalism, said that he doesn’t think many students will be interested in earning the certificate.

“I think there’s a lot of fear and animosity towards artificial intelligence right now and I’m not saying it’s misplaced,” Banville said. “I think that there are real questions that need to be asked about it.”

He said that the School of Journalism offered a free, one-day, one-credit course on AI last spring and about 15 students, much fewer than he expected, showed up for it.

Banville said he hopes that the certificate will be more successful in finding an audience and that students will not want to turn away from talking about AI because of the politics of data centers.

“Whether a data center gets built in Bonner or not, these tools are out there and they are going to change your life,” Banville said. “I just want you to be ready and have the tools to decide how and when and when not to use it.”
